John Craig
jon krayg
proper noun
From the Scots and Gaelic creag, “rock, crag”; the given name John from the Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”

Biblical Definition

John Craig (c. 1512–1600) was a colleague of John Knox and a chief labourer in the founding of the Reformed Kirk of Scotland. Once a Dominican friar, he was brought out of Rome by the reading of Calvin’s Institutes, was condemned by the Inquisition at Rome and marvellously delivered on the eve of his execution, and returned to his native land to preach the gospel he had once opposed. Standing alongside Knox in Edinburgh, he ministered the Word with steadfastness and afterward served as chaplain to King James VI. His most enduring gift to the church was Craig’s Catechism of 1581, a plain and faithful summary of Reformed doctrine drawn up for the instruction of the young and the establishing of the flock in sound teaching, and the National Covenant of 1580 in large part flowed from his pen. His life bears witness that the LORD can reclaim a man from the deepest error of Rome and make him a herald of free grace, that catechising is no small labour but the sowing of the Word in tender ground, and that the doctrine which delivers a soul from bondage becomes the doctrine he must faithfully teach. He counted no former station too high to renounce for the truth as it is in Jesus.

Webster 1828 Definition

Reformer and colleague of Knox, delivered from Rome and author of Craig’s Catechism.

expand to see more

John Craig (c. 1512–1600), Scottish Reformer and fellow labourer with John Knox in Edinburgh.

A former Dominican friar converted by reading Calvin’s Institutes and delivered from execution by the Roman Inquisition.

Author of Craig’s Catechism (1581), a plain instrument for instructing the young in Reformed doctrine.

A principal framer of the National Covenant of 1580, binding the nation to the true religion.

Later royal chaplain to King James VI, faithful in the pulpit to the end of his long life.

Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of sound catechetical teaching.

expand to see more

John Craig is preserved because the church has largely forgotten the labour of catechising, that patient sowing of sound doctrine into young and unstable souls which he counted worth a lifetime. His deliverance from Rome and his devotion to plain teaching stand as a rebuke to an age that prizes novelty over the diligent handing down of the faith once delivered.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Craig is the discipline of catechetical instruction, the deliberate teaching of doctrine to the young and the whole flock that they may not be tossed about by every wind. His conversion out of Rome by the pure exhibition of Reformed truth witnesses to the power of doctrine faithfully set forth, and his catechism preaches that the Reformation was a recovery of the Word from centuries of corruption, not merely one voice among many.

Hebrew Roots

The name is bound up with the founding of the Scottish Kirk and the recovery of catechetical instruction.

expand to see more

Craig’s deliverance from Rome shows the Reformation as rescue from corruption, not a matter of preference.

His catechism roots the young in the doctrines of grace, guarding them from later error.

His partnership with Knox planted the Reformed Kirk on the sure foundation of the Word.

His hand in the National Covenant bound Scotland to the true religion under God.

His long ministry preaches perseverance in teaching sound doctrine to the very end.

Usage

"Craig’s Catechism is remembered as an early and faithful instrument of Reformed instruction in Scotland."

"His conversion by the Institutes is cited as a witness to the converting power of sound doctrine."

"He is named among the founding fathers of the Scottish Reformation beside Knox."
